'Let not your heart be troubled (mē tarassesthō): ye believe in God, believe also in me' Cyril notes the deliberate parallel of objects of faith: 'believe in God' and 'believe in me' (pisteuete eis ton Theon, kai eis eme pisteuete). This verse is the textual foundation of Cyril's Trinitarian theology.

'My Father is greater than I' (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin) is THE most contested verse in Cyril's John commentary — the Arian polemical favorite throughout the 4th century, requiring careful orthodox exposition. Cyril resolves through the standard distinction: the verse predicates 'greater' of the Father with respect to the assumed humanity of the incarnate Son, NOT with respect to the eternal divine nature. Insofar as the Son is incarnate (took on human nature), the unincarnate Father is 'greater' in mode-of-existence; insofar as the Son is eternal Word, He is consubstantial-equal with the Father. The verse therefore confirms rather than denies the incarnation, and presupposes rather than undermines the consubstantiality. This careful exposition is one of Cyril's most-cited Johannine passages in later Greek theological tradition.

'I am in the Father, and the Father in me' (egō en tō Patri, kai ho Patēr en emoi) is for Cyril the foundational Johannine text for what later Greek theology would call perichoresis: the mutual indwelling of the Persons of the Trinity. The reciprocal 'in' (en) preserves the Personal distinction (the Son is not the Father, the Father is not the Son) while affirming the consubstantial unity (each is fully in the other by virtue of the one shared divine essence). 'The words that I speak unto you, I speak not of myself' (continuing the verse) Cyril reads not as denial of personal agency but as expressing the unbroken Trinitarian operation: the Father's words come through the Son in the Spirit. This verse is the textual foundation of Cyril's Trinitarian theology.

'I will pray the Father, and He shall give you another Comforter (allon Paraklēton), that He may abide with you for ever' is for Cyril the principal Johannine text on the personal divinity of the Holy Spirit. 'Another' (allon — implying same-kind-as) Cyril stresses: the Spirit is the same KIND of divine Person as Christ is — not a different ontological category, not a lesser being, not merely impersonal divine power. 'Paraklēton' Cyril expounds as advocate/comforter/encourager/intercessor — all four functions belong to the Spirit because they all belong to the divine Person. 'Abide with you for ever' establishes the permanence of the post-Pentecost Spirit-indwelling (as distinct from the intermittent prophetic-inspiration of the Old Covenant economy).

The world's incapacity to receive the Spirit Cyril attributes not to ontological lack but to the cognitive condition of unbelief that blocks perception. 'Ye know Him' (gnōskete) Cyril emphasizes as the disciples' present-tense possession of pneumatic knowledge — even before Pentecost, in nascent form. The eschatological 'shall be in you' (en hymin estai) Cyril reads as the post-Pentecost completion of what is here proleptically begun. Cyril's pneumatology of progressive economy (already present in the verse) becomes systematic in his On the Holy Trinity dialogues.

The Tewahedo Anaphora's epiclesis prayers explicitly invoke this triple participation as the gift the eucharistic communion realizes in the worshipper.

'But the Comforter, which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in my name, He shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you' is for Cyril the locus classicus for the apostolic-authority basis of Scripture and Tradition. The Spirit's twin functions (teach + remind) presuppose the prior content given by Christ; the Spirit does not invent new revelation but illuminates and consolidates what Christ has spoken. This grounds Cyril's argument against any sectarian claim to revelation beyond the apostolic deposit: the Spirit's teaching is bounded by what Christ taught. The Tewahedo doctrine of the inseparability of Scripture-and-Tradition (Mäṣḥafä Hēnok + Mäṣḥafä Qǝddase together with the Tanakh + NT) rests on this Cyrilline reading.

'My Father is greater than I' (ho Patēr meizōn mou estin) is THE most contested verse in Cyril's John commentary — the Arian polemical favorite throughout the 4th century, requiring careful orthodox exposition. Cyril resolves through the standard distinction: the verse predicates 'greater' of the Father with respect to the assumed humanity of the incarnate Son, NOT with respect to the eternal divine nature. Insofar as the Son is incarnate (took on human nature), the unincarnate Father is 'greater' in mode-of-existence; insofar as the Son is eternal Word, He is consubstantial-equal with the Father. The verse therefore confirms rather than denies the incarnation, and presupposes rather than undermines the consubstantiality. This careful exposition is one of Cyril's most-cited Johannine passages in later Greek theological tradition.
